citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI.
creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Microsoft Research AI, Carnegie Mellon University, University of Washington)
description: PIQA (Physical Interaction: Question Answering) is a benchmark dataset for evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding systems. Given a physical goal expressed in natural language, a model must choose the most sensible solution from two options. The dataset contains over 16,000 training QA pairs with additional development and test sets, and is designed to test knowledge of physical properties, affordances, and object manipulation.
name: PIQA (Physical Interaction: Question Answering)
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr according to both self-reporting on turkerview.com and timing calculations. Annotators were required to pass a qualification HIT with >80% accuracy before participating in the main annotation task.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human performance was calculated by majority vote on development data, achieving 94.9% accuracy. Annotators chosen for human evaluation achieved 90% on the qualification HIT. Examples with low annotator agreement were removed from the dataset during validation. The sentence length distributions for correct solutions and tricks were found to be nearly identical, and vocabulary overlap between correct and incorrect solutions was at least 85% across noun, verb, adjective, and adverb categories.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) — inferred from use of HITs (Human Intelligence Tasks) and reference to turkerview.com for pay reporting
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were shown an instructable and asked to: (1) provide a physical goal (often centered on atypical materials), (2) provide a valid solution, and (3) provide a "trick" — a solution that sounds reasonable but is subtly wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. A qualification HIT was run prior to the main annotation stage; annotators had to achieve >80% accuracy on well-formed and underspecified (goal, solution) pairs to participate. Data was collected in batches and validated by other annotators for correctness. Users with low agreement were de-qualified. A diff button was included in the interface to highlight differences between solutions. Annotators were seeded with instructables from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop. Two examples were drawn per instructable. During validation, examples with low agreement were removed.
rai:dataBiases: Reporting bias was identified as a major concern: when thinking about how to achieve a goal, people are most often drawn to prototypical solutions and common tools (e.g., kitchen or garage items), rarely considering the hundreds of other everyday objects. To address this, annotators were prompted with instructables links to encourage thinking about atypical uses of everyday objects and flatten the distribution of referenced objects. The AFLite algorithm was applied to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples that could artificially inflate model performance. The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT to avoid easy exploitation of annotation artifacts.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected using instructables.com as a scaffold. Annotators were prompted with links to instructables (crowdsourced how-to instructions covering categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop) and asked to construct goal-solution pairs. Annotators provided a physical goal, a valid solution, and a "trick" (a subtly incorrect solution). Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness. The dataset was further cleaned using the AFLite algorithm to remove annotation artifacts and spurious biases.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructions from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of how-to instructions covering topics from cooking to car repair. In most cases, users provide images or videos detailing each step and a list of required tools. Annotators used these instructables as inspiration to construct goal-solution pairs.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, User-generated content data
rai:dataLimitations: During validation, examples requiring expert-level knowledge of a domain (e.g., special woodworking terminology) were removed as they do not fall under "commonsense." The dataset focuses on everyday situations and may not cover specialized physical knowledge. The paper notes that future research may "match" humans on the dataset by finding a large source of in-domain data and fine-tuning heavily, but this is not the intended use. Physical commonsense knowledge is inherently limited in text due to reporting bias.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The AFLite algorithm was applied to remove annotation artifacts and spurious biases. AFLite uses 5,000 examples to fine-tune BERT-Large and computes embeddings of all remaining instances, then uses an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets to identify and discard instances whose feature representations are highly indicative of the target label. Text was tokenized using Spacy for statistics. The GPT BPE tokenizer was used for sequence length analysis. The train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance AI systems' ability to understand physical commonsense, which is critical for day-to-day human life including problem solving. The authors argue that modeling physical commonsense knowledge is a major challenge on the road to true AI-completeness, including robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. The benchmark is intended to elicit further research into building language representations that capture details of the real world.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking progress in physical commonsense understanding for natural language understanding systems. Evaluating language representations on their knowledge of physical commonsense (physical properties, affordances, and object manipulation). Probing the inner workings of deep pretrained language models to determine the extent of their physical knowledge. Advancing language representations that capture knowledge traditionally only seen or experienced, to enable construction of language models useful beyond the NLP community, including robotics applications.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite algorithm using BERT-Large (fine-tuned on 5,000 examples) for computing embeddings used in bias reduction. Spacy tokenizer used for text statistics. GPT BPE tokenizer used for sequence length analysis.

null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described; the dataset consists of text QA pairs with no missing value filling.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection data manipulation (augmentation, resampling, balancing) is described beyond the AFLite filtering already captured in preprocessing.
